title: Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree
prompt:
Given an integer array `nums` sorted in strictly ascending order, build a height-balanced binary search tree from it and return it.

A height-balanced tree is one where the depths of the two subtrees of every node never differ by more than 1. If multiple valid answers exist, any of them is accepted, but the checker in this exercise expects a specific canonical construction: always pick the middle element (rounding down for even-length ranges) as the subtree root. Since this is a coding exercise rather than an interactive class-based design, the function returns the built tree serialized to a level-order array (`null` for missing children) using the provided `tree_to_level_order` helper.

examples.explanation: The middle element 0 becomes the root; [-10,-3] builds the left subtree and [5,9] builds the right subtree, recursively picking the lower-middle index each time.
With two elements, the middle index rounds down to index 0 (value 1), making 3 the right child.

constraints: nums is sorted in strictly increasing order
hints: Since the array is already sorted, the in-order traversal of any BST built from it must reproduce the array — that constrains how you can split it.
Pick the middle element of the current range as the subtree root, then recursively build the left subtree from the left half and the right subtree from the right half.
For an even-length range, consistently choose the lower middle index (mid = (left + right) // 2) so the split matches the expected canonical shape.

solution.approach: Recursively build the tree from a subarray range [left, right]: pick mid = (left + right) // 2 as the root value (rounding down for even-length ranges to match the expected canonical answer), then recursively build the left subtree from [left, mid-1] and the right subtree from [mid+1, right]. Because nums is sorted, this always keeps every left-subtree value smaller and every right-subtree value larger, and always balances since each recursive call halves the range.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(log n) recursion stack, O(n) for output
